claims.text: The studied material is equiatomic, Co-free FeNiCrMn.
The alloy has a homogeneous, defect-minimized, as-solidified microstructure.
The Co-free alloy maintains a strength–ductility balance similar to Co-containing high-entropy alloys.
The dynamic mechanical response of solidified FeNiCrMn is controlled by competition between dislocation pile-up and thermally activated dynamic recovery.
Dislocation pile-up, local lattice distortion, and possible short-range-order clusters mediate strain hardening.
Low temperature and high strain rate limit dislocation mobility.
Limited dislocation mobility produces dislocation pile-up and localized strain hardening.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate deformation may be accompanied by short-range ordering.
Dislocation pile-up and localized strain hardening increase strength while reducing ductility.
Elevated temperature and lower strain rate facilitate thermally activated dynamic recovery and dislocation annihilation.
Dynamic recovery reduces strength and enhances ductility.
FeNiCrMn will exhibit higher strength and lower ductility at low temperature and high strain rate.
FeNiCrMn will exhibit lower strength and improved ductility at higher temperature or lower strain rate.
The proposed study varies temperature from approximately -100 °C to 300 °C and strain rate from approximately 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^3 s^-1.
Quasi-static room-temperature behavior of as-solidified FeNiCrMn serves as the baseline.
The hypothesis is restricted to homogeneous solidified samples without significant secondary-phase formation.
Substantial segregation or extraneous defects may cause deviations from the predicted behavior.
TEM and in-situ imaging can be used to relate strength and ductility changes to pile-up, recovery, dislocation density, and local ordering.
Failure of temperature or strain rate to correlate with the predicted dislocation structures and strength–ductility shift would falsify the proposed mechanism.
